nameStory: The butternut gets its common name from the rich, buttery flavor of its edible nuts, which were prized by Native Americans and early settlers. It's also called "white walnut" because its wood is much lighter in color than its cousin, the black walnut. The scientific name "cinerea" means "ash-colored," referring to the pale gray bark that makes this tree easy to spot in the forest.
description: Butternut is a medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 40-60 feet tall with a broad, open crown. It belongs to the walnut family and produces edible nuts encased in sticky, elongated husks. The tree has distinctive compound leaves with many leaflets and pale gray bark with deep furrows. Unfortunately, butternut populations have declined dramatically due to a fungal disease called butternut canker.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Pale gray to light brown bark with distinctive diamond-shaped ridges and deep furrows that create a crosshatched pattern. The bark feels rough and corky to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with 11-17 pointed leaflets arranged along a central stem. Each leaflet is 2-4 inches long with serrated edges and a fuzzy, slightly sticky texture underneath.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Oblong nuts about 2 inches long, covered in a sticky, fuzzy green husk that stains your fingers yellow-brown. The nuts are ridged and pointed at one end, unlike round walnuts.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Medium-sized tree with a short trunk and wide-spreading, irregular crown. Branches often grow at odd angles, giving the tree a somewhat scraggly appearance.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are fuzzy, grayish-brown, and noticeably flattened on top. The terminal bud (at the branch tip) is much larger than side buds and has a distinctive heart shape.

habitat: Butternut grows in rich, well-drained soils of mixed hardwood forests, often on slopes and along stream valleys. In New England, you'll find it mixed with sugar maple, basswood, and other hardwoods, typically at lower to middle elevations. It prefers partial shade to full sun and is often found along forest edges and old farm boundaries.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge late in spring, and small greenish flowers appear in drooping clusters called catkins. Male and female flowers grow on the same tree but look quite different.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage provides identification through large compound leaves, and developing nuts begin forming in their sticky green husks.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, and mature nuts fall to the ground still enclosed in their husks. This is harvest time for the edible nuts.
seasonality.winter: Bare trees show the distinctive pale gray, diamond-ridged bark and fuzzy, heart-shaped terminal buds that make winter identification possible.

funFact: Butternut husks were historically used to dye Confederate uniforms a brownish color during the Civil War, leading to Southern soldiers being nicknamed "Butternuts" - a term that had nothing to do with their diet but everything to do with their clothing!
confusionNotes: Butternut is most often confused with black walnut, but butternut has much lighter gray bark (versus dark brown-black), and its nuts are oblong and sticky rather than round. Memory trick: "Butternut = light bark, black walnut = dark bark."
contextualKnowledge: Butternut trees are critically endangered in much of their range due to butternut canker disease, a fungal infection that kills trees within years of infection. Many states have special protections for remaining healthy butternut trees, making them increasingly rare treasures in New England forests.
compareHints: Among the walnut family members in New England, butternut is easily distinguished from black walnut by its pale gray bark and oblong, sticky-husked nuts versus black walnut's dark bark and round nuts. Persian walnut (English walnut) is mainly found in cultivation and has smoother, lighter bark and thinner-shelled round nuts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to butternut, its closest New England relative, black walnut has more leaflets per compound leaf, smooth (not sticky) leaf stems, and rounder nuts versus butternut's elongated nuts.
Persian walnut differs from our native black walnut and butternut by having smooth-edged leaflets (not serrated), lighter gray bark, and round nuts (butternut has oblong nuts).
Japanese walnut differs from our native black walnut in having a generally more northern cold tolerance and different nut characteristics.
